query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: At high operating temperatures, the overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation of the FeNiCrCoCu coating are governed by the in situ formation of a thin, adherent, nanocrystalline oxide layer (rich in Cr and Cu) during sliding. This oxide layer acts as a load-bearing barrier and suppresses localized plastic shear, reducing wear.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu coating deposited in the as‐deposited state with a fine nanocrystalline microstructure and minimal pre‐formed oxides.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled post‐deposition annealing treatment (e.g., 600°C for 1 hour in air) to promote the oxidation of Cr and Cu, while keeping all other coating parameters identical to the baseline.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding regime (approximately 600°C) under fixed load and sliding speed, representative of the intended operating conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A nanocrystalline oxide film that forms in situ on the coating surface, enriched in Cr and Cu oxides.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, selective oxidation of Cr and Cu creates a thin, adherent oxide tribolayer. This layer distributes the applied stress during sliding and limits dislocation nucleation at the coating surface, thereby mitigating severe localized plastic deformation and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline as‐deposited coating, the annealed coating will exhibit a lower wear rate and a more uniform, distributed pattern of microscopic deformation due to the load-sharing effect of the protective oxide film.
generation.baseline: The as‐deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating, which has not undergone post‐deposition annealing and therefore has minimal pre‐formed protective oxide on its surface.
generation.boundary: This prediction holds under high-temperature (≈600°C) sliding conditions with similar applied loads and speeds. Effects may be different at much lower temperatures or under substantially different mechanical loading conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact composition, thickness, and mechanical properties of the in situ oxide layer and how these factors quantitatively affect wear resistance remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coated substrates: (a) the baseline as‐deposited coating and (b) identical coatings subjected to a post‐deposition annealing treatment at 600°C for 1 hour in air. Conduct sliding wear tests at 600°C under identical loads and speeds. Characterize the oxide film formation using surface microscopy (SEM/EDS) and measure wear rates and friction coefficients.
measurements: Wear rate (e.g., mass loss, volume loss, wear scar dimensions)
Oxide layer thickness and elemental composition via SEM/EDS or XPS
Microstructural analysis of deformation (e.g., via TEM or EBSD)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a distinguishable, continuous oxide film or if they show no improvement (or a deterioration) in wear resistance and deformation uniformity compared to the baseline as‐deposited samples, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions.
